paper_style.palette_strategy: Figure 1 uses pastel categorical labels for Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code. Figures 2–4 use viridis-like sequential heatmaps with a shared vertical Mean Accuracy [%] colorbar per figure. All tables use black/white booktabs-style rules with bold/underline ranking and explicit TokenLimit text.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Figures 1–4 contain embedded RGB raster image objects; surrounding captions, text, and all tables/rules are PDF vector objects. No editable plotting/table source was found.
paper_style.style_consistency: Heatmaps and result tables are internally consistent in panel/row grammar, dataset ordering, and caption placement. Figure 1 is a separate interface-illustration sub-system; embedded raster fonts and the heatmap palette are not fully unified with the Nimbus/Computer Modern page system.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Illustration of the LLM-graph interaction strategies described in Section 3.1.

color.semantic_mapping: Green, blue, and pink dashed rounded labels identify Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code; neutral tones draw graph/data/agent/code icons.

encodings.x: Ordered flow from graph data/instructions to the LLM and its interaction surface.
encodings.color: Green, blue, and pink dashed labels identify Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code.
encodings.shape: Icons and rounded boxes distinguish graph data, instructions, agent, actions, and pandas code.
encodings.line: Arrows encode the direction and feedback loop of interaction.
encodings.text: Panel labels and object names directly identify the three modes.

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual interface diagram; no measurements, samples, accuracy values, uncertainty, or statistical aggregation.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 3 formalizes node classification and Figure 1 makes the three interaction contracts visible before Tables 1–3 compare their outcomes; it does not by itself establish a performance advantage.
design_strengths: Isomorphic left-to-right flows make the access/operation distinction quickly scannable.
Color, labels, icons, and spatial position redundantly identify the modes.
design_weaknesses: Small internal labels are difficult at page scale.
The figure does not show each mode’s exact visible resource set, token budget, call count, or failure path.
Pastel category colors are not fully grayscale-safe.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a shared input→LLM→operation skeleton to compare agent interfaces, while annotating the actual resource/access contract and runtime budget.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Accuracy of 2-hop prompting and Graph-as-Code on the cora, arxiv, and cornell datasets under varying ratios of randomly removed edges and truncated text features.

color.semantic_mapping: viridis-like sequential intensity maps Mean Accuracy [%] from low/dark purple through green to high/yellow; cell numerals give the same value.

encodings.x: Feature Deletion [%], five levels from 0 to 100.
encodings.y: Edge Deletion [%], five levels from 0 to 100 with the rendered vertical orientation.
encodings.color: Sequential cell fill encodes Mean Accuracy [%] and the shared vertical colorbar defines the scale.
encodings.facet: Columns are cora, arxiv, cornell; rows are Prompting and Graph-as-Code.
encodings.text: Every 5×5 cell contains a numeric mean-accuracy annotation; row labels and panel titles are direct labels.

figures.data_and_statistics: Each cell is the mean accuracy over five independent runs, predicting 1,000 randomly sampled test nodes per seed; edges are uniformly randomly removed and features are token-truncated. No spread/error is drawn.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 5.1’s feature-versus-structure dependency experiment; the matched surfaces support shared/deviating dependence and robustness readings, but access contracts remain unmatched because Graph-as-Code can query a broader DataFrame than Prompting.
design_strengths: Shared axes and colorbar make six panels directly comparable.
Numeric cell labels preserve exact approximate values when color differences are hard to see.
The matrix exposes dataset-specific collapse and robustness regions.
design_weaknesses: Dense 5×5 labels and small tick text are hard to read after page scaling.
No seed dispersion, deletion realization, or feasibility/TokenLimit mask is shown.
Sequential color is not fully grayscale-safe.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use the same 2D perturbation grid for each treatment and dataset, with shared color scale plus numeric cell labels; add an explicit uncertainty or feasibility layer for deployment claims.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Accuracy of 2-hop prompting and Graph-as-Code on the photo dataset under varying ratios of randomly removed edges and truncated features.

color.semantic_mapping: viridis-like sequential intensity maps Mean Accuracy [%] from low/dark purple through green to high/yellow; cell numerals give the same value.

encodings.color: Shared sequential colorbar encodes Mean Accuracy [%].
encodings.facet: Two vertically stacked panels for Prompting and Graph-as-Code on photo.
encodings.text: Cell values, row labels, axis labels, and panel placement directly label the comparison.

figures.data_and_statistics: The 5×5 surfaces use the same five-run mean and 1,000 test nodes per seed protocol as Figure 2; no dispersion is shown. The very low Prompting surface can include context-window feasibility failure, not only feature dependence.
figures.evidence_relation: The photo case in §5.1 connects long text/high degree and context-window TokenLimit to the divergence between Prompting and Graph-as-Code; Tables 6–7 quantify the related token/latency cost.
design_strengths: Compact two-panel inset keeps the dataset-specific failure explanation beside the relevant text.
Shared axes/colorbar preserve the Figure 2 grammar.
design_weaknesses: Right-float width makes ticks and cell numerals especially small.
No explicit TokenLimit mask or context-window boundary separates infeasibility from accuracy.
No uncertainty or deletion realization is visible.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a dataset-specific failure mode, reuse the global deletion-surface grammar in a compact inset and add a separate status encoding for non-runnable cells.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Accuracy of 2-hop prompting and Graph-as-Code on the cora, arxiv, and cornell datasets under varying ratios of randomly removed edges and known labels.

color.semantic_mapping: viridis-like sequential intensity maps Mean Accuracy [%] from low/dark purple through green to high/yellow; cell numerals give the same value.

encodings.x: Label Deletion [%], five levels from 0 to 100.
encodings.y: Edge Deletion [%], five levels from 0 to 100.
encodings.color: Sequential cell fill encodes Mean Accuracy [%] with a shared vertical colorbar.
encodings.facet: Columns are cora, arxiv, cornell; rows are Prompting and Graph-as-Code.
encodings.text: Cell numerals, row labels, dataset titles, and axis labels directly expose the comparison.

figures.data_and_statistics: Each cell is a five-run mean over 1,000 randomly sampled test nodes per seed; labels and edges are uniformly randomly deleted. No uncertainty, permutation realization, or query-trace summary is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 5.2’s label-versus-structure dependency analysis; the surfaces support the reported relative stability and dependency shift, but adaptive reliance is not directly observed at trace level.
design_strengths: Reusing Figure 2’s panel geometry makes feature/label dependency families easy to compare.
Shared color scale and numeric cells support cross-dataset and cross-mode scanning.
design_weaknesses: Caption does not define the scope of “known labels.”
No uncertainty, deletion realization, or resource-access control is visible.
Dense raster labels and color scale degrade in grayscale/thumbnail use.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep a fixed panel template across perturbation families so only the treatment axis changes; pair surface plots with matched-access trace evidence before making causal mechanism claims.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Accuracy of baselines and LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code on short-text homophilic datasets. Best per-dataset results are bold, runner-up underlined.

tables.uncertainty: mean ± undefined spread; no interval or test
tables.data_and_statistics: Accuracy is reported as mean ± an undefined spread for four short-text homophilic datasets; the top four rows provide # Classes, average text length, homophily, and average degree. Products/2-hop prompt is TokenLimit.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 4.1 Findings 1–2 use this baseline→mode matrix to compare short-text homophilic performance; the table does not alone establish significance.
design_strengths: Metadata is colocated with outcomes.
Common row order makes baseline and mode comparison fast.
Bold/underline gives each dataset a local ranking cue.
design_weaknesses: The ± quantity, denominator, and run aggregation are not defined.
TokenLimit has no local threshold/footnote.
Small table text and rank-only emphasis hide effect magnitude/stability.
tables.reusable_pattern: Put dataset descriptors above baseline and treatment rows, retaining explicit best/runner-up and non-runnable states while defining the dispersion and budget in the caption.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Accuracy of baselines and LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code on heterophilic datasets. Best per-dataset results are bold, runner-up underlined.

tables.uncertainty: mean ± undefined spread; no interval or test
tables.data_and_statistics: Accuracy is mean ± an undefined spread for cornell, texas, washington, and wisconsin; metadata rows report classes, text length, homophily, and degree. Texas/2-hop prompt is TokenLimit.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 4.2 Finding 3 uses the table to test whether all interaction modes remain effective in heterophilic graphs against trivial and label-propagation baselines.
design_strengths: It reuses Table 1’s row grammar, enabling regime comparison.
Homophily and degree rows contextualize the heterophilic setting.
Bold/underline gives a compact per-column ranking.
design_weaknesses: The spread and runs are undefined.
A TokenLimit cell lacks an explanatory footnote.
Non-monotonic mode behavior needs prose; no local effect-size or uncertainty cue.
tables.reusable_pattern: Reuse a fixed regime-specific results template while changing dataset columns and metadata, and define failure-state semantics in the table caption.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Accuracy of baselines and LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code on long-text homophilic datasets. Best per-dataset results are bold, runner-up underlined.

tables.uncertainty: mean ± undefined spread; TokenLimit for non-runnable cases
tables.data_and_statistics: Accuracy is mean ± an undefined spread for six long-text homophilic datasets; metadata rows report classes, text length, homophily, and degree. 2-hop prompt frequently becomes TokenLimit, while 2-hop budget prompt is the resource-limited comparison.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 4.3 Finding 4 uses the table to connect long text/high degree with prompting feasibility and Graph-as-Code performance; Tables 6–7 quantify costs.
design_strengths: Explicit TokenLimit entries prevent silent missingness.
Budget prompt provides a visible resource-aware baseline.
Six datasets expose domain breadth in one grid.
design_weaknesses: The widest table has the smallest text.
The failure threshold and ± statistic are undefined.
Feasibility failure and accuracy are mixed in one cell grid, complicating causal interpretation.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep performance and explicit failure states together in long-text tables, but add a separate budget/token panel and define all aggregation states.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Accuracy of LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting and Graph-as-Code across LLMs of varying sizes.

tables.uncertainty: mean ± undefined spread; some TokenLimit cells
tables.data_and_statistics: Two method groups (2-hop prompt and Graph-as-Code) report mean ± an undefined spread on seven datasets plus an average row across Llama, o4-mini, DeepSeek R1, and GPT-5; some cells are TokenLimit.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix B.1 uses this scale/family matrix to extend the main o4-mini results; it supports persistence across named models but does not isolate parameter scale from family/configuration.
design_strengths: Model columns and method groups make the scale sensitivity scanable.
Bold average rows provide a compact cross-dataset summary.
The same dataset-by-mode semantics are retained.
design_weaknesses: Model family, parameter scale, and API/reasoning configuration change together.
Spread and TokenLimit semantics are not defined.
No token/latency matching accompanies the accuracy comparison.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use method-group × model-condition × dataset with an average row, and add cost/feasibility columns when interpreting model-size effects.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Accuracy of LLM-graph interaction strategies Prompting and Graph-as-Code across LLMs with reasoning and non-reasoning modes.

tables.uncertainty: mean ± undefined spread; no paired uncertainty
tables.data_and_statistics: Two interaction groups report mean ± an undefined spread on seven datasets plus average under Phi-4 and Qwen, each split into without-reasoning/reasoning columns; average rows are bold.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix B.2 Finding 12 is a within-family reasoning toggle ablation; it connects to model-size Table 4 and cost Tables 6–7, but no token-matched control is visualized.
design_strengths: Two-level family × reasoning header makes the paired contrast explicit.
Repeated dataset rows allow within-mode and within-family scans.
Average row gives a concise summary.
design_weaknesses: Reasoning may change output length and latency, but those costs are absent.
No dispersion definition, difference column, or failure summary.
Small multi-level header increases lookup effort.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use family as the top header and capability toggle as the second header, with paired cost and accuracy summaries.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Average token counts per query for each LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool and Graph-as-Code over long-text datasets.

tables.data_and_statistics: Average integer tokens/query for reddit, photo, and wiki-cs across five interaction variants; no dispersion or input/output/cached-token breakdown is shown.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix C.1 quantifies the context-window mechanism behind Table 3 TokenLimit and Figure 3 photo divergence; it pairs with latency Table 7.
design_strengths: Compact dataset × mode layout makes order-of-magnitude growth visible.
Column names align with the accuracy tables.
Thousands separators aid scanning.
design_weaknesses: Tokenizer and token accounting are unspecified.
No distribution, tail, budget line, or input/output split.
The caption does not delimit exact variant names beyond the table columns.
tables.reusable_pattern: Align resource metrics to the same dataset/mode keys as accuracy results and report budget plus distributional tails.

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7: Average latency (wall-clock time in seconds) per query across for each LLM-graph interaction modes over long-text datasets.

tables.data_and_statistics: Average wall-clock seconds/query for reddit, photo, and wiki-cs under 2-hop prompt, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code; wiki-cs 2-hop prompt is TokenLimit and no dispersion/percentiles are shown.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix C.2 checks whether token-efficient interaction modes also change end-to-end latency; it supplies a deployment boundary for the main accuracy story.
design_strengths: Unit and timing metric are explicit in the caption.
Short table preserves a clear three-mode comparison.
TokenLimit is visible rather than silently omitted.
design_weaknesses: No concurrency, warm-up, API scheduling, network, or percentile protocol.
Mean-only values cannot show stability or tail risk.
Caption contains a grammatical “across for each” ambiguity.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair accuracy and token tables with a latency table using identical dataset/mode keys, then report protocol and percentiles.

tables.label: Table 8

caption.text: Table 8: Accuracy of LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, Summary Prompting, GraphTool, and Graph-as-Code on long-text datasets. Best per-dataset results are bold, runner-up underlined.

tables.data_and_statistics: Point accuracy for seven prompting/summary/tool/code rows across six long-text datasets; best and runner-up are bold/underlined, while TokenLimit remains a category. No dispersion is shown.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix D.1 tests the exposure-only alternative: multi-hop summary prompting versus adaptive Graph-as-Code. It directly extends the long-text comparison in Table 3.
design_strengths: Summary rows share columns with original prompt rows, shortening the comparison path.
Ranking and TokenLimit jointly show performance and feasibility.
The row groups make the alternative explanation explicit.
design_weaknesses: This appendix table switches to point accuracy rather than the main tables’ ± format.
Summary token/latency cost is not paired.
Caption does not define the summary aggregation.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place original exposure, summarized exposure, and adaptive access in shared columns, while keeping uncertainty conventions consistent across tables.

tables.label: Table 9

caption.text: Table 9: Accuracy of baselines and LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool and Graph-as-Code on datasets with randomly shuffled adjacency matrices.

tables.data_and_statistics: Point accuracy after ten independent random adjacency permutations on seven representative datasets; node features and degree distribution are retained, meaningful structure is destroyed. No dispersion is shown.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix D.2 is the structure-versus-code-prior control; compare with Tables 1–3 to read degradation, but the table has no paired original/shuffled delta.
design_strengths: Covers short-text, heterophilic, and long-text regimes in one control matrix.
Caption identifies the adjacency perturbation.
Method and dataset order is compatible with the main results.
design_weaknesses: No original/shuffled paired column or degradation marker.
Permutation count and spread are not encoded in the table.
Cross-table comparison is required to see effect magnitude.
tables.reusable_pattern: Reuse the benchmark column order for a control table, adding original/shuffled paired deltas or a compact difference view.

tables.label: Table 10

caption.text: Table 10: Mean Squared Error (MSE) of LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool and Graph-as-Code on the synthetic shortest path prediction task across varying true path lengths (k).

tables.data_and_statistics: Point MSE at k=1,2,3,4,≥5 and aggregate k≥1 for 2-hop prompt, GraphTool+, and Graph-as-Code; no uncertainty or stratum counts are shown.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix D.3 turns the interface distinction into a synthetic computation-boundary test; perfect Graph-as-Code values support executable BFS within this task only.
design_strengths: Path-length columns make the fixed-context cutoff visible.
Aggregate k≥1 gives a quick overall comparison.
Small table has a short scan path.
design_weaknesses: No per-stratum sample counts, variance, or graph/pair sampling detail.
Two-decimal 0.00 may conceal residual error.
Synthetic task grants generated code a direct algorithm-execution advantage.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use problem-complexity strata as columns for interface mechanisms, and report sample counts and tool/execution boundaries beside perfect scores.

tables.label: Table 11

caption.text: Table 11: Accuracy comparison between classic GNNs, hybrid LLM+GNNs, and our evaluated LLM-graph interaction modes Prompting, GraphTool and Graph-as-Code on long-text datasets.

tables.uncertainty: point accuracy; no dispersion; external rows imported from Wu et al. (2025)
tables.data_and_statistics: Point accuracy for three architecture groups: 2 classic GNN, 4 hybrid LLM+GNN, and 5 LLM-only rows across five long-text datasets; imported GNN/hybrid values and in-paper LLM-only values are mixed, with no uncertainty.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix D.4 contextualizes zero-shot LLM-only results against supervised architectures; it narrows the “best interaction” claim to the frozen LLM-only scope rather than a matched randomized comparison.
design_strengths: Architecture-family row groups make scope context visible.
Long-text dataset columns align with the main comparison.
Compact groups avoid repeating long family names in every row.
design_weaknesses: External/imported values are not visually marked.
Training budget, preprocessing, split and protocol alignment are absent.
Point-only values do not convey stability.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use architecture row groups for scope context, but mark external rows and state protocol alignment in caption/footnote.

tables.label: Table 12
tables.data_and_statistics: Fourteen datasets are grouped into short-text homophilic, heterophilic, and long-text homophilic regimes; columns list nodes, edges, classes, and Train/Val/Test percentages. No uncertainty applies.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix G supplies the dataset index for Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–4, connecting regime labels and scale/split context to every result object.
design_strengths: All dataset names, regimes, sizes, classes, and splits are consolidated in one stable reference.
Comma-separated integers and split percentages are easy to scan.
The same regime grouping used in the results is visible.
design_weaknesses: Caption does not state data sources, homophily definition, or split convention.
The rendered regime label is embedded alongside dataset names without a separate header.
No link to the exact preprocessing or sampling protocol is shown.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep a regime-grouped dataset statistics table as the appendix index and add source, definition, and split footnotes.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 defines the three information-interaction surfaces; Tables 1–3 compare them across short-text homophilic, heterophilic, and long-text homophilic regimes; Figures 2–4 turn the comparison into feature/edge/label dependency surfaces; Tables 4–7 add model, reasoning, token, and latency axes; Tables 8–11 add summary, shuffled-structure, synthetic-algorithmic, and supervised controls; Table 12 indexes the datasets.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All captions start with Figure/Table n. Figures 2–4 state metric, methods, datasets, and perturbations, while Figure 1 relies on its panel labels and Section 3.1. Tables 1–3 and 8 define best/runner-up styling; most other captions describe setup but omit spread, repetition, or failure-state definitions.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Main tables use dataset columns and baseline/interaction rows, with metadata rows above outcomes. Appendix headers switch to model-family/reasoning columns, resource-mode columns, path-length strata, or architecture row groups. Horizontal booktabs-style rules and no vertical rules consistently encode groups.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 1’s interface contract leads to Tables 1–3 accuracy; Figures 2–4 test input-dependency surfaces; Tables 6–7 quantify token/latency constraints; Tables 8–11 test exposure-only, structure-noise, algorithmic, and supervised alternatives. The visual chain is strong, but Graph-as-Code and Prompting do not expose matched resource sets.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main pages carry interface, three regime results, and deletion heatmaps. Appendix Tables 4–5 extend model/reasoning axes, Tables 6–7 quantify cost, Tables 8–11 provide controls, and Table 12 supplies dataset context; non-tabular Example 1/Templates 1–3 explain the Graph-as-Code access contract without adding counted Figures/Tables.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Nimbus Roman No9 L and Computer Modern math are stable for page text, captions, and tables. Raster heatmap internals use an estimated sans-serif, while the appendix code templates use Nimbus Mon; table typography is more consistent than figure-internal typography.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Pastel categorical mode labels are stable only in Figure 1; Figures 2–4 consistently use a sequential viridis-like accuracy scale; tables remain monochrome and use weight/underline. Local semantics are coherent, but there is no single palette token across interface and heatmap sub-systems, and grayscale recovery is incomplete.

most_reusable_patterns: Figure 1’s shared three-way input→LLM→operation skeleton for comparing interaction contracts.
Figures 2–4’s matched 2D deletion surfaces with fixed dataset columns, method rows, shared colorbar, and numeric cell labels.
Tables 1–3’s metadata→baseline→interaction template with explicit TokenLimit and best/runner-up cues.
Appendix row groups and multi-level headers that separate model scale, reasoning, summary exposure, shuffled structure, algorithmic difficulty, and architecture scope.
Tables 6–7’s alignment of token and wall-clock cost with the same dataset/mode keys used by accuracy tables.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1: establishes the three access/operation interfaces.
Table 3: exposes long-text feasibility and TokenLimit alongside accuracy.
Figures 2–4: provide the main dependency and robustness surfaces.
Tables 8–9: make exposure-only and structure-noise alternative explanations directly comparable.
Table 12: provides the dataset/regime reference needed to interpret all result objects.
failure_patterns: Figures 2–4 omit seed dispersion, deletion realizations, and an explicit TokenLimit/feasibility layer.
Tables 1–5 use an undefined ± quantity while Tables 8–11 switch to point accuracy, weakening cross-table statistical comparability.
Captions are generally not self-contained; Figure 3 is especially small as a right float and Table 12’s caption is only a title.
Table 11 mixes imported supervised results with in-paper LLM-only values without a visual source/protocol marker.
No public plotting, table-generation, or LaTeX source was found, so source-level visual reproducibility is unavailable.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Define the three interaction interfaces with Figure 1, connect cross-regime accuracy tables to matched deletion heatmaps, and use appendix scale/reasoning/cost/control tables to expose feasibility, alternative explanations, and dataset scope.
